children.text: The Native Village of Mekoryuk: Bering Sea Observation and Monitoring from a Local Perspective

The Native village of Mekoryuk wants to share its knowledge of the Bering Sea with the western research community. We also want to increase our capacity to do western style research and therefore participate with other researchers in the North Pacific Marine Research Project.  Our Elders have seen great changes and have a tremendous amount of knowledge that needs to be recorded.  This information will be very useful for other researchers and will be made available to them, provide it is used appropriately.  It has been traditional to make observations about what one sees in the environment and to share these observations with others in the village - this is how we survived.  In today's busy world this communication is not happening as much and observations are going untold and therefore unrecorded in our oral tradition.  This project would reopen sharing about observations and would record them in a western scientific way.

An NPMR project

children.text: Creating a Bering Sea Council of Elders for Stewardship in the Bering Sea

Indigenous peoples, including the Aleut, Inupiat, Ittelman, Koryak, Siberian Yupik, and Alaska Yupik, have coexisted with the Bering Sea for over eight thousand years, living successfully by their understanding of the winds, tides, currents, climate, and sea ice to harvest fish and wildlife. Such traditional knowledge and wisdom long ago taught Alaska Natives that in order to thrive they must assume an active stewardship role with the land, the sea, and all its creatures. Through time, the Bering Sea has come to mean everything to coastal peoples: it is the spiritual, cultural, physical, and economic centerpoint of their lives. In the most profound sense, this sea and the people who live along its coast have become one.  As outside organizations identify research priorities and management decisions are being made, it is critical that Bering Sea coastal people, whose lives remain wholly dependent on an abundant and diverse marine ecosystem, have an active role in understanding the problems and policies affecting them, and to
decided what steps they need to take. However, because the coastal residents are organized into community, sub-regional, and regional groups, there is no forum for collective decisions on an ecosystem-wide basis. The Council of Elders' leadership is
necessary to unify and prioritize the research goals of the region's Native peoples.

An NPMR project
A proposal for NPMR to establish A Bering Sea Council of Elders for stewardship in the Bering Sea.

children.text: Green Seafood - Alaska Sea Grant Radio Show

As consumers, many of us want to know that the products we buy won't harm the environment or us. That's especially important when it comes to seafood, since much of the seafood we eat still comes from the ocean. A labeling program that lets consumers know if the fish they eat comes from well-managed stocks is having an impact in Alaska. As Doug Schneider reports in this week's Arctic Science Journeys Radio, one Alaska fishery has met the program's certification standards, but another faces opposition from environmentalists.

Some people might remember the controversy more than a decade ago over dolphins killed by tuna fishermen in the South Pacific Ocean. The flap ended only after the industry agreed to fishing methods that reduced dolphin deaths. As an incentive, companies that sold tuna caught with such methods could market the catch as dolphin safe. Such labeling was a hit among consumers and launched an era of so-called "green" labeling. 

 More recently, Alaska seafood has gotten in on the trend. 

In December, Alaska salmon became the first U.S. fishery certified as environmentally friendly by the Marine Stewardship Council, a nonprofit organization that uses green labeling as a way to improve fisheries management. Jim Humphreys is the U.S. director of the Marine Stewardship Council.

children.text: Quarterly Brad-scale Surveys Off Central and Southern Oregon and Northern California

4 transect lines off Oregon and northern California are sampled three times per year as part of the U.S. GOBEC program, in April, July and September.  The time series began in July 1997 and will continue through 2003.  Transect lines include Newport OR (44°40N), Coos Bay OR (43°13'N), Rogue River ORE (42°30'N) and Crescent City CA (41°54'N).  The transect lines extend beyond the continental shelf to 160 km from shore (2900 m water depth) off Newport; Coos Bay to 63 km from shore (1700 m); Rogue River to 64 km from shore (3060 m depth); and Crescent City to 150 km from shore (3400 m depth).  At each station CTD casts are made.  At most stations nutrients and chlorophyll are sampled from 9 discrete depths, and zooplankton is sampled with the vertical tow net from 100m to the surface.  Bongo tows were made at most stations in 1998 and 1999.  Beginning in March 2000, zooplankton were collected from discrete depths using a 1 sq. m MOCNESS system.  WOCE drifters are released at five stations along the Newport Line (10. 15. 25. 45 and 65 miles from shore).  On each cruise underway measurements are made of currents (ADCP), and fish and zooplankton acoustics using an HTI 244 system.  In addition to the coast-wide sampling, the Newport Line is sampled in February and November, giving us five visits per year to the deep ocean along that line.

Prince William Sound Nowcast-Forecast System (PWS NFS)

The PWS NFS has both modeling and observational components, and utilizes both new and existing monitoring sites. The observational network includes 2 NDBC buoys, 3 NDBC C-MAN stations, 3 NOS tide gauge stations, 3 hydrographic stations, ADCP transects, satellite-tracked drifting buoys, and a GEM-EVOS sponsored ADCP mooring at Hinchinbrook Entrance. The observational network has recently been expanded to include 4 more meteorological stations. Additionally, sampling of nekton and plankton is carried out at various sites throughout the sound. Archived and near real-time data and model simulations will soon be publicly available on a web site.
Observations include water temperature, salinity, water level, tides, currents, plankton and nekton net surveys, wind speed/direction/gust, atmospheric pressure, air temperature, and dew point.

children.text: About 30 nations participated in the observational program, using ships to make physical and chemical observations, and employing moored and drifting instrumentation. Global observations were also made from satellites. The field phase of the project lasted from 1990-1998 and was followed by Analysis, Interpretation, Modeling and Synthesis activities. This, the AIMS phase of WOCE, officially continued to the end of 2002.

Data include bathymetry, current meters, drifters, sub surface floats, air-sea fluxes, hydrography, profiling floats, satellite sea level, satellite sea surface temperature, satellite surface winds, sea level - delayed mode, sea level - fast return, sea surface salinity, shipboard ADCP, surface meteorology, and upper ocean thermal.
The NOAA NODC web site provides WOCE data and summaries at http://woce.nodc.noaa.gov/wdiu/.  DVD WOCE Global Dataset Version 3.0 can be ordered from NODC at http://www.nodc.noaa.gov/woce_v3/.

The World Ocean Circulation Experiment (WOCE: http://www.woce.org/) was a component of the World Climate Research Program (WCRP) and remains the most ambitious oceanographic experiment undertaken to-date. The aims of the program were to establish the role of the oceans in the earth's climate and to obtain a baseline dataset against which future change could be assessed. Sophisticated numerical ocean models were also developed to provide a framework for the interpretation of the observations and for the prediction of the future ocean state.

children.text: University of Washington (UW, School of Oceanography and College of Education)

The Puget Sound Marine Environmental Modeling (PSMEM) is a project of a partnership of five separate organizations, collectively operating or developing four dynamic, predictive models of the Puget Sound's aquatic environment and one biogeochemistry module. Each model has a different spatial coverage with a goal to integrate the modeling efforts into a coordinated whole.

To develop quantitative understanding of Puget Sound's circulation and marine ecosystem, and of the sensitivity of the physical and the biological system to natural and human perturbations; and to develop models of the Sound that can aid agencies with responsibilities for environmental management in making informed decisions and serve as marine science education tools.

The Pacific Ocean Shelf Tracking (POST) project aims to build an acoustic tracking array along the west coast of North America. The early applications focused on tracking the migration, life span, movement and behavior of Pacific salmon. The project is expanding to encompass other species such as rockfish, sturgeon and small pelagics.
